conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night with severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… it was the worst pain ever. Crampy, all over my stomach. I’ve had pain before, but this was different—like twisting and burning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned some back pain too, wrapping around your right side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right flank. And I feel pain everywhere—head, back, stomach. Plus nausea. I haven’t vomited, but I feel sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your labs showed a very high white blood cell count—24.2—so we’re looking for infection. But your CT scan didn’t show anything like appendicitis or a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? But I’ve been having bowel movements—big ones yesterday and today. Still feel like I need to go but can’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. The X-ray shows a lot of stool in your colon, but also, we just got a stool test back—it’s positive for C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: C. diff? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bacterial infection in the colon. It can cause severe diarrhea and cramping. Even though you’re not having constant diarrhea now, it can start with constipation and then shift.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I did take Amitiza recently for constipation. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Amitiza can increase bowel movements, and in people with gut changes—like from cirrhosis—it might increase risk. We’re going to stop it for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. So what’s the treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on oral vancomycin, which treats C. diff directly in the gut. We may add another antibiotic through your IV if the diarrhea worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your pain, labs, and bowel movements. If things improve, maybe 5–6 days. But we need the infection under control first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is coming down—from 24 to 18. That’s a good sign the infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had more diarrhea today—every 20 minutes or so. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common with C. diff, especially early in treatment. We’ve added IV metronidazole to help control it faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel weak. And my blood pressure was low last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were a bit dehydrated from the diarrhea. Your sodium was low—135. We’re giving fluids and watching closely. It’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this related to my liver disease?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cirrhosis makes you more vulnerable to infections like C. diff. But your liver function is stable—bilirubin and enzymes are okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ascites? I didn’t feel swollen, but I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed no ascites. So no need for paracentesis. But we held your diuretics—furosemide and spironolactone—because your blood pressure was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to restart them later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as an outpatient. Your liver team will guide that. You’re being evaluated for transplant, so they’ll want to keep your fluid balance in check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea is slowing down, and your white count is now 14. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little better. But still achy. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Inflammation can cause body aches. But we also checked your old MRI—you have a small mass near your spine at T10.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they said it’s a neurogenic tumor, stable. Could that be causing pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but it hasn’t changed in size. Right now, we think your abdominal pain is mostly from C. diff. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your white count is down to 11.6, and you’ve only had two loose stools today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I do feel less crampy. So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re going to keep the vancomycin but switch to oral only. You no longer need IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? I was on iron for anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue iron supplements. Your ferritin was very low—9—so you’re still deficient. An outpatient infusion is scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain meds? Tramadol helps, but I know it can cause constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it as needed. But we’re also continuing your bowel regimen—Miralax and lactulose—to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day—we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the full course of vancomycin—it tapers over four weeks. Take it exactly as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—four times a day the first week, then twice, then once, then every other day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re stopping Amitiza. It may have contributed to the diarrhea. Your regular bowel meds—Miralax, lactulose, docusate—are fine to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my water pills—furosemide and spironolactone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Don’t restart them yet. Your blood pressure was low. Call your liver doctor—they’ll tell you when to resume.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start swelling or short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then call your doctor right away. Those could be signs of fluid buildup. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. You’re alert, walking, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it was C. diff and not something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we caught it early. Keep taking the vancomycin, restart your diuretics when told, and follow up with your PCP and liver team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I have more diarrhea or pain, I’ll call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done really well. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine culture showed contamination, so no UTI. And your asthma and depression meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’m using my inhaler as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep taking citalopram and risperidone. Mental health is important, especially with chronic illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. It’s been hard, but I’m trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’re all here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications. Then you can head home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—hand hygiene is key. C. diff spreads easily. Wash well, especially after using the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. No one else in my house is sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That helps. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You’re here because you were confused and had worsening abdominal pain. Do you remember coming to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I felt really foggy. I couldn’t think straight. The pain in my belly and back got worse suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You were a bit disoriented when you arrived—only aware of yourself. We think this is related to your liver condition, called hepatic encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s happened before. Is it because of an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You had a fever and low blood pressure, and your white blood cell count was high. We’re treating you for a presumed infection in the belly, possibly related to your cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like the C. diff I had last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked, but the stool sample was too formed for the C. diff test. So we stopped the vancomycin. Your recent diarrhea might have been from the lubiprostone, which was already stopped after your last discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the infection now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see any clear source. No pneumonia, no UTI, no abscess. But your symptoms and labs suggest an infection, so we started IV antibiotics—ceftriaxone—to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood pressure? I felt so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low, but it improved after IV fluids. That’s a good sign. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also noticed my stools were black the past few days. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your rectal exam—no blood, and the test was negative. The black color might be from something you ate or iron, but we’ll keep an eye on your hemoglobin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My back pain still bothers me—it goes from my neck down my left leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. You have a known mass near your T10 spine. The CT shows it’s unchanged—likely a benign nerve tumor. It could be contributing to the pain, but it’s not new or worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my belly? It’s still swollen and tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver disease causes fluid buildup, but this time, there’s no ascites. The tenderness may be from your chronic IBS or constipation. The CT showed no blockage or stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this pain for years. Is there anything new we can try?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding off on new meds now. But after discharge, your GI doctor will start linaclotide, once insurance approves it. It’s for constipation-predominant IBS.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds hopeful. What about the encephalopathy? I feel a bit clearer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good—you’re more alert already. We’ve been giving lactulose every two hours to help clear the toxins your liver can’t handle. We’ll keep adjusting it until you’re fully oriented.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are improving. White count is down, and you’ve had no more fevers. Blood cultures show no growth so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Does that mean the infection is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s looking that way. We’ll switch you to oral antibiotics—levofloxacin—for two more days at home. That completes a five-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to take anything long-term for infections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since we couldn’t confirm the infection type and you don’t have ascites, we’re not starting long-term prophylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my liver? I’m still on the transplant list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still listed. Your MELD score is stable. We’ll continue your usual meds—rifaximin, lactulose, PEG—and monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking tramadol for pain. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using acetaminophen instead. Tramadol can affect your mental status, especially with encephalopathy. We’ll keep pain control gentle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My vision’s still blurry in one eye—should I see a specialist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It’s been stable—likely related to your glaucoma medication. Keep using your travoprost and follow up with your eye doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Blood pressure is stable, you’re fully alert, and your abdomen is much less tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll send you home with two doses of levofloxacin to finish the antibiotic course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my constipation meds? I don’t want another flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue docusate, senna, magnesium, and PEG. Linaclotide will start at your GI follow-up—just need approval first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diuretics? I usually take them for fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We didn’t restart them this time because your blood pressure was low. Your liver doctor will decide when to resume them safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics—any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Levofloxacin is usually well-tolerated. But if you get diarrhea, dizziness, or rash, stop it and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when should I go to the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you become confused again, have a fever, severe pain, or trouble breathing, come right back. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, and you’re doing great. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What’s the plan when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds except the antibiotics—take one pill daily for the next two days. Your son will help you, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’s picking me up and will check in daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Follow up with your liver and GI doctors. They’ll manage your transplant status and start the new IBS medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to keep those appointments. I’m glad I’m on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and keep up with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at the next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch with your outpatient doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I feel much more like myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep working on your recovery at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m ready to get back to my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just take it slow. Listen to your body and stay in touch with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. Can you tell me your name?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m Ms. Thompson. I came in because my face was drooping and my right arm felt weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned some facial droop and right-sided weakness. When did this start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started a few days ago. My sister noticed my face looked off. At first I thought it was just tiredness, but then my arm got weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And is the weakness getting better or worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My arm is a little better, but my leg still feels heavy, like I’m dragging it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You also mentioned some numbness on the right side of your face?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s like a tingling, not sharp pain. And my speech feels a bit slurred sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I noticed that too. We’re going to check for a stroke, but first I need to do a quick exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see mild drooping on the right side when you’re at rest, but when you smile, it looks even. That’s interesting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It comes and goes. One nurse said it looked like the left side was drooping earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’re going to get a CT scan of your head right away to rule out a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news — no sign of a stroke, bleeding, or any acute brain issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stroke? Then what is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Because your symptoms are changing and the scan is normal, we’re going to do an MRI for a closer look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI results are in. Like the CT, there’s no evidence of a stroke, tumor, or aneurysm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I really felt weak. It wasn’t in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. But the neurology team reviewed everything and thinks your symptoms may be related to your liver condition — hepatic encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before, but I thought I was past it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Encephalopathy can come and go. It can affect your brain function, sometimes causing confusion, speech changes, or even odd neurological symptoms like weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the face droop and arm weakness could be from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Your exam shows some lingering numbness and mild weakness, but no stroke. We’re going to treat this as encephalopathy for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your lactulose to four times a day to help clear toxins from your system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It helps, but it’s not fun.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. But it’s important to keep your mental clarity and prevent worsening. We’ll monitor how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’m a little clearer. The numbness is still there, but I don’t feel as foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs this morning show your liver enzymes were a bit high yesterday, but they’re coming down today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not ideal, but it’s improving. We did an ultrasound of your liver — no ascites, and blood flow is normal. So nothing new there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood culture that came back positive?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That showed viridans streptococci, but only in one bottle. It’s likely a skin contaminant, not a real infection. You’ve had no fever, so we’re not treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re making progress. Your mental status is better, and your strength seems more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can think more clearly. But I still feel clumsy with my right hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The numbness and mild weakness may take time to resolve. Since your scans are clean, we’ll focus on managing the encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your liver tests are trending down again. We’re confident this was encephalopathy flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll send you home with lactulose four times a day and a follow-up with your primary doctor in three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I still take my omeprazole? I’ve been on it a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend reviewing that with your doctor. PPIs like omeprazole can increase infection risk in cirrhosis if not truly needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tramadol for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can continue it as needed, but avoid opioids and benzodiazepines — they can worsen encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used benzos before for anxiety. Should I stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Best to avoid them. Talk to your psychiatrist about safer options. Citalopram and hydroxyzine are okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Will the numbness go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should improve over time. Keep taking the lactulose and follow up with labs — CBC, chem-7, LFTs, and coagulation panel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant status?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still listed. This episode doesn’t change that. Your MELD score is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if you feel more confused, weak, or unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see my doctor in three days for the labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll fax the results there. You’re cleared to go home with services as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is glad you’re feeling better. Stay safe, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — my right eye is still blind, but that’s old, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s chronic and unchanged. No new vision issues. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Ms. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in from rehab because of confusion and worsening hallucinations. Can you tell me how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little better. The voices and shadows are still there, but not as bad. I was so scared last night. They said my pain meds might be part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we think the oxycodone and Flexeril may have made your confusion worse. We’ve stopped both. You’re also on risperidone for hallucinations, which helps, but we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know those could affect my mind. I just took them for back pain. Is that why I couldn’t think straight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. We also found signs of a urinary tract infection. That can worsen confusion, especially with your liver condition. We’ve started antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t feel like I had a UTI. No burning or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common, especially in older adults or those with chronic illness. Symptoms aren’t always typical. Your urine test showed infection, so we’re treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach and back still hurt. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding opioids now. They can worsen confusion and constipation. We’ve started a new medication called lubiprostone for your bowel movements, and you can take Tylenol for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this pain for years. Is it from my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver is enlarged, which can cause discomfort. But your pain seems more related to chronic constipation. The lubiprostone should help. We’ll see if your pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my face? It drooped last time, and sometimes I can’t feel the left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your last admission. The MRI and CT showed no stroke. Your symptoms come and go, even when you’re asleep they’re gone. Neurology thinks it’s not a nerve problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it? It feels real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be related to stress or your overall health. Your liver disease affects your brain function. We call that hepatic encephalopathy. It can cause odd symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver is making me confused and my face droop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. This time, we think the infection and meds made it worse. We’re treating the UTI and keeping you off sedating drugs. Your mental clarity has already improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your kidney function was a bit low when you came in—creatinine up to 1.2. But after fluids, it’s back to 1.0. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it was just dehydration. Your liver disease makes you sensitive to fluid changes. We’ll keep encouraging you to drink and eat well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My white blood cell count is high. Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was 13.6, which is high, but it’s likely from the UTI and also from not eating much. When you’re dehydrated, counts concentrate. We’ll repeat it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest X-ray? I saw something about a spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test came back negative, so we don’t need to treat for that. Your urine culture grew mixed bacteria, but since you’ve had VRE before, we’re sticking with ampicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I still need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for one more week. Even though the culture was mixed, we’re finishing the course because of your history. It’s oral, so you can take it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the lubiprostone—is that working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve had regular bowel movements and your pain is better. We’re glad we could avoid opioids. They can make constipation and confusion worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today show your ammonia level is normal, and you’re alert and oriented. That’s a big improvement from when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. But sometimes my face still feels numb on the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted that. It comes and goes, and there’s no nerve damage on imaging. It may be related to how your brain processes sensation, especially under stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I see a psychiatrist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not recommending that now. But if symptoms worsen, your primary doctor can help decide if a referral is needed. For now, we focus on your liver and overall health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll finish the ampicillin, keep taking lactulose and rifaximin for your liver, and stay on the lubiprostone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m going back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to extended care. They’ll help with your daily needs. We’re also sending reminders to avoid opioids and benzodiazepines—they can trigger confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the mass on my spine? The MRI mentioned it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small benign tumor, likely a schwannoma. It hasn’t changed in size. You’ll need a yearly MRI to monitor it, but it’s not causing symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant evaluation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s still ongoing. Your MELD score is stable. Continue with your liver team for follow-up. Avoid alcohol completely—it’s crucial for your candidacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a drink in months. I want this chance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your commitment matters. We’ll keep supporting you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go. Your mental status is clear, infection is treated, and pain is controlled without opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What signs should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you become confused again, have fever, or your face droops and doesn’t improve, come back. Also, finish all your antibiotics and keep your follow-up labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no pain pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use Tylenol and tramadol only if absolutely needed. Avoid oxycodone. It’s safer for your liver and brain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had black, tarry stools for two days. And I spit up something dark yesterday. I felt shaky in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s called melena, and it usually means there’s bleeding in the upper part of your digestive tract. We also saw your blood sugar was low in the ER—50—which explains the shakiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But I didn’t feel dizzy or confused this time, like last time. Is it my liver again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You have cirrhosis, which increases your risk for bleeding, especially from varices—swollen veins in the esophagus. But your last EGD three months ago didn’t show any. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got a unit of blood in the ER, right? My pressure dropped too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure dipped to 87/55, likely from the blood loss or the pain medication you got. We gave fluids and one unit of blood, and your pressure came back up. No further drops since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My back pain is still here, but I’m used to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage that with your usual tramadol and lidocaine patch. But right now, the priority is making sure the bleeding has stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What tests will I have?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already started labs. Your hemoglobin is 10.6, which is low but stable. We’ll repeat it. We also gave you octreotide to reduce blood flow to the liver and prevent variceal bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got ceftriaxone as a precaution. With cirrhosis, we worry about infections, especially spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, even if you don’t have ascites right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My white count is high again, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 12.5, but that’s been up before. No fever or signs of infection now. Your urine culture showed mixed flora, likely contamination, so no UTI treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another round of antibiotics unless I need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs overnight show your hemoglobin went up to 11.3, and your white count dropped to 9.2. That’s a good sign—no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does that mean I don’t need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GI team reviewed your case. Since you’re stable and improving, they don’t think an urgent EGD is needed. But we may do one later to check your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait—my last EGD didn’t show varices. Could it still be that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Varices can develop quickly in cirrhosis. But even if they’re there, if there’s no active bleeding, we may not need to treat them right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My kidneys—are they okay? Last time I was here, my creatinine went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 1.3 on admission—up from your baseline of 1.0. Likely due to volume loss from the bleed. With IV fluids, it’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not kidney failure this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acute failure. Just a temporary rise. We’re monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you to the regular floor today. Your hemoglobin is stable at 10.9, and creatinine is down to 1.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your regular diet. We also scheduled an EGD for tomorrow to check your stomach and esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they treat anything if they see it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If they see active bleeding or high-risk varices, yes. But if it’s quiet, they’ll just take a biopsy if needed and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back from your EGD. Good news: no active bleeding. But there are now two small varices in your esophagus—grade 1.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So they showed up since last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, which isn’t uncommon with cirrhosis. They didn’t treat them because they’re low risk. But we’ll keep you on omeprazole and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They saw redness throughout your stomach—gastritis—and took a biopsy. We’ll get results in a few days. Could be from alcohol, medications, or just cirrhosis itself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a drink in months. I’m still in the transplant program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know, and that’s great. The gastritis might not be from alcohol. We’ll keep you on sucralfate and omeprazole to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your AST and ALT are normal, bilirubin is low—0.2. That’s good. Your liver function is stable despite the cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my face? Last time I was here, I had drooping on one side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neuro exam is normal now. No facial droop or weakness. Those episodes before were likely not stroke-related, given no changes on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was scared it was a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were too, but everything points to it being something else—maybe neurological fluctuations from your liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your labs this morning are good: hemoglobin 10.9, creatinine 0.9, white count 6.7. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? Really? I feel okay, but I was worried about the bleeding coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The risk is low now. You’re not actively bleeding, your vitals are stable, and your labs are improving. We’re sending you home with ciprofloxacin for two days as extra infection prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can keep using tramadol as needed. And we added a short course of trazodone at night for sleep, since you mentioned insomnia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And I need to follow up with my liver doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially for the biopsy results and your transplant evaluation. Call if you have black stools, dizziness, or belly pain that gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work staying off alcohol. That’s the best thing for your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m trying. It’s hard, but I want that transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re on the right track. We’ll support you every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my back pain. It’s still there. Should I see someone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your primary or pain specialist can help. There’s a paraspinal mass on old imaging, but it hasn’t changed. We’ll make sure your records go to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I feel better knowing we’re watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in because of black, tarry stools and feeling lightheaded. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.text: I was worried it might be another bleed. Last time, I almost passed out.

conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs, and your hemoglobin is 11.3, which is a bit low but stable compared to your last admission. No signs of severe anemia or shock.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do an EGD tomorrow morning — that’s a scope of your stomach — to check for varices or ulcers. We also ordered a Doppler ultrasound of your liver today.

conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It’s not too bad. But I was told there was food in my stomach last EGD — I couldn’t fast well.

conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you don’t eat after midnight. We need a clear view. We also plan a colonoscopy to rule out lower GI bleeding.

conversation_lines.text: Both? I hope it’s not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s better to be thorough. With cirrhosis, bleeding can come from several places. We want to find it — or rule it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The liver ultrasound is back. It shows your cirrhosis is still there — nodular liver, atrophic left lobe — but no new masses or blood clots. Your liver vessels are open and flowing normally.

conversation_lines.text: No clots? That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. Portal vein thrombosis is a risk in cirrhosis, but you don’t have it. Your spleen is a bit enlarged, which is expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the back pain? Could that be from the tumor near my spine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI from before showed a small 1.7 cm mass, likely benign. It hasn’t changed. It might contribute, but your pain is probably multifactorial — musculoskeletal and chronic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from your scopes. The EGD showed grade 1 esophageal varices — small, not bleeding — and normal stomach lining. But there was food in your stomach, so the view wasn’t perfect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry. I was nervous and had a snack before coming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It happens. The good news is no active bleeding or ulcers. The colonoscopy was also normal — no bleeding sources in the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So where’s the black stool coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see active bleeding, but you did have melena. We did a capsule study — you swallowed a tiny camera — to look at your small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot about that. When will we know the results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It takes a few days. But since your hemoglobin is stable and you haven’t had more black stools, it’s likely not active bleeding now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to watch you a bit longer and make sure you’re stable. We’ll check your labs again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.text: Is that drop bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: So still no answer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I was off my water pills.

conversation_lines.text: And sucralfate?

conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that twice daily. It coats your stomach and helps protect it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain? I’m still uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been anxious about this whole thing.

conversation_lines.text: I understand. Keep taking your citalopram and risperidone as prescribed. We don’t want stress making things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re being discharged today. Your condition is stable, no active bleeding, and you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I see black stools again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted for weakness. Can you tell me more about how you've been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve been really tired for a few days. I’ve had black stools again and some lightheadedness when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your stools are still black and tarry? Any bright red blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mostly black, but I saw a little red in the bowl the other day. Not a lot. I’ve been having about 4–5 bowel movements a day since I restarted lactulose after my last discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. That could be contributing. We checked your labs, and your hemoglobin is low at 8.1, which is down from your last discharge. That explains the fatigue and dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from bleeding again? I was just here two weeks ago for something similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that serious? My kidneys were okay last time.

conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I stop the lactulose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about my belly swelling again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed no new ascites, so that’s good. Your liver looks as expected for cirrhosis, but no fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why am I still bleeding? They didn’t find anything last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pill camera? I did that before. It didn’t show anything.

conversation_lines.text: Alright. And what about my blood? Will I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.text: I used to take omeprazole. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few days, likely. We need to see your kidney numbers improve and get the capsule study results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still tired, but the dizziness is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I got really lightheaded. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: So they didn’t find anything again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, weekly CBC and basic metabolic panel. Fax the results to Dr. Patel’s office. We need to watch your hemoglobin and kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you so much for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Just nervous about the bleeding coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: So it’s still bleeding a little?

conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?
